extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, curriculum developers, and secondary/college mathematics teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for designing, researching, and implementing instruction that develops mathematical thinking, problem solving, and enculturation into mathematical practice. Covers classroom practices, curriculum design, assessment, research methods, and teacher preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher as facilitator (deflect authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: The teacher should not act as an all-knowing authority but as someone who asks pointed questions to help students arrive at correct mathematical judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deflect undue authority from the teacher and place the burden of mathematical judgment (with constraints) on students. Instructor plays facilitating and critical rather than show-and-tell role; withhold immediate presentation of solutions to develop community argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of social interaction and group conflict to create mathematical tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit small-group work and inter-group reporting that produces conflicting results so students must resolve tensions and make mathematical issues salient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give groups same or different problems (e.g., measuring the same triangle), have groups report varied answers, prompt resolution through discussion and comparison, and use ensuing conflict to prepare students for theoretical discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pose conjecture-and-argument questions rather than 'prove that' tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Present problems as 'what do you think is true, and why?' instead of standard 'prove that' assignments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage students to conjecture, state what they are willing to accept, and then justify their assertions. This supports student-led discovery and mirrors mathematical research practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students engage in doing mathematics consistent with epistemology
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must do mathematics in a way consistent with the instructor's mathematical epistemology, reflecting on connections between classroom formal reasoning and reasoning outside class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities should require reflection on doing mathematics and on connecting formal classroom reasoning to outside contexts; include debates, definition-building, and argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definition exploration and counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Have students propose, defend, and refine definitions, using counterexamples (illustrative figures) to rule out inadequate definitions until a correct definition emerges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than providing definitions, invite students to suggest alternatives and use concrete examples/figures to test and eliminate inadequate candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom as a community jury for mathematical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure class so claims about mathematical properties must be defended and judged by the student community, with the teacher as an especially knowledgeable member rather than sole authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitate student argumentation and reflection on the nature of argumentation itself (e.g., validity of inductive proofs, converses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce mathematical tools via meaningful complex problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Major mathematical topics should be motivated and introduced by significant problems (often from physical sciences) from which mathematical tools meaningfully evolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use real-world motivated problems (e.g., gravitational attraction problem to introduce the Riemann integral) and allow tools to emerge from problem discussion rather than presenting cut-and-dried formalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induce metacognitive reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should be induced to reflect on their own thought processes as part of learning mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks and classroom discourse that prompt students to articulate and analyze their strategies, decisions, and reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enculturation into mathematical community and practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop students' mathematical perspectives, values, and identities through interactions with members of mathematical communities and participation in community practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on legitimate peripheral participation, social interactions, and practices that move students from peripheral to fuller participation; study how community membership shapes mathematical point of view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curricular units in large coherent chunks
rubrics_metrics.description: Lessons and units should be sizable coherent chunks (e.g., 2–6 weeks) motivated by meaningful problems and integrated across subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid isolating topics (e.g., teach algebra and geometry separately); use projects and problems that require simultaneous use of multiple domains; favor extended collaborative projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom practices from California framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific recommended teacher behaviors: model problem-solving, create comfortable atmosphere, invite explanation at all stages, allow multiple strategies, use rich problem situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model exploring and experimenting with students; encourage risk-taking; solicit student explanations throughout problem solving; recognize that problems may require original approaches and multiple strategies; present rich, transferable problem situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment must measure what is important ('what is tested is what gets taught')
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessments should align with the goals of mathematical power; current standardized multiple-choice tests are inadequate for most desired skills and perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop assessment measures at individual and school/district levels that capture broad skills (reasoning, problem solving, communication, collaboration), not just narrow subject-matter mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and design of open-ended questions with reliable informative scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Open-ended items can provide rich information but require scoring procedures that are reliable and informative to assessors and students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks that require understanding and communication (example: giving directions over the phone to recreate figures). Investigate what information can be gleaned and develop scoring rubrics that balance reliability and informativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portfolios as assessment artifacts and their structuring
rubrics_metrics.description: Student portfolios (best work, collaborative project records, role descriptions) can document learning but must be structured and evaluated fairly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide what entries to require (e.g., proudest problem solved, record of group work) and develop transparent, fair evaluation guidelines for portfolio assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Videotaped collaborative problem solving as an assessment source
rubrics_metrics.description: Videotaping small-group work on difficult open-ended problems may yield inferences about students' collaborative experience and strategic fluency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research whether trained observers can reliably detect prior collaborative experience or strategic fluency within minutes of viewing; develop reliable observational methods and inference rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational definition requirement for 'problem solving' research
rubrics_metrics.description: Every study or discussion of problem solving should include an operational definition of the term and examples of what is meant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify whether problem solving refers to routine exercises, contest performance (e.g., Putnam), or developing a mathematical point of view; avoid umbrella usage that groups contradictory behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research methods need explicit fit/guidance ('user's guides')
rubrics_metrics.description: Research methodologies should come with explicit guidance on what aspects of problem solving they address, caveats, and what they are unreliable for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide method-specific notes: suited explorations (A,B,C), caveats, and known limitations (D,E,F). Example: protocol parsing useful for Webster's type 2 problems but not for routine tasks and not revealing underlying mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and appropriate uses of protocol parsing
rubrics_metrics.description: Protocol parsing (analyzing protocols from non-interventive problem solving) documents presence/absence of executive decisions and consequences, but is useful mainly for 'perplexing or difficult' problems and reveals little about underlying mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interventive methods when probing why individuals made particular choices; recognize that interventive probing disturbs natural problem flow and changes appropriateness of parsing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for improved representations of domain knowledge (resources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Better descriptions and representations of cognitive/knowledge structures are needed, and a clearer account of how resources interact with strategies, control, beliefs, and practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work toward congruence between descriptive models of knowledge structures and phenomenological sense of their functioning; study dynamic interactions among components of problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy instruction: describeability and learnability, research on training and transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem solving strategies can be described in detail and are learnable; research should determine the nature and amount of training needed and the extent of transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct controlled studies on training dosage, problem types for training, and measures of transfer to other tasks or domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization and development of control processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Control (self-regulation/executive decisions) lacks adequate theoretical characterization and understanding of development and domain-dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop theoretical models of control mechanisms, investigate whether control is domain-independent or domain-dependent, and study how children develop analogous self-regulatory skills in math compared to social contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beliefs and affect require new conceptual and methodological work
rubrics_metrics.description: Beliefs and affect are under-conceptualized; existing measurement tools are inadequate and often only indicate that something happens without explaining how or why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop new methodologies and explanatory frames to meaningfully integrate cognition and affect or to explain why integration may not be possible; move beyond 'telling good stories' toward mechanistic explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research on enculturation and learning practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding how mathematical practices are learned (enculturation) is crucial but currently supported mainly by a few case studies; theoretical and methodological tools are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expand tools to study social issues (how biases and perspectives are picked up), elaborate concepts like legitimate peripheral participation, and develop detailed accounts of what people learn and why within communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher professional development intensity and systemic support
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers can change classroom behavior with appropriate in-service experiences (weeks of intensive study rather than one-day workshops); systemic structures must support teacher change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the kinds of teacher knowledge and behaviors needed to implement ambitious curricula at scale, investigate how teacher beliefs form and evolve, and research district/school structures that enable sustained change.
